analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $7.15 and extends it to the Northern Mariana Islands.
analysis.headline: A Republican-sponsored bill to raise the minimum wage from $5.15 to $7.15 never received a hearing or vote and died in a House subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the federal minimum wage in three steps — $6.00 within 60 days, $6.75 on January 1, 2006, and $7.15 on January 1, 2007 — up from $5.15, where it had sat since 1997. It also would have applied the federal minimum wage to the Northern Mariana Islands, which had been exempt, phasing workers there up from $3.55 an hour. It was introduced by a Republican, drew only Republican cosponsors, and never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning the $5.15 federal minimum wage — concentrated in restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service jobs — would gain up to $2.00 an hour, about $4,160 a year for a full-time worker once fully phased in. Workers in the Northern Mariana Islands, then outside the federal wage floor, would gain a minimum wage for the first time and a guaranteed path to the federal level.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers earning the $5.15 federal minimum wage

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in three steps — $6.00 within 60 days of enactment, $6.75 on January 1, 2006, and $7.15 on January 1, 2007 — worth about $4,160 more per year for a full-time worker compared with the $5.15 floor.

Extends the federal minimum wage to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, which had been exempt, starting workers there at $3.55 an hour and raising the wage by $0.50 every six months until it reaches the federal level.
Phases the mainland increase in quickly, with the first $0.85 raise arriving just two months after enactment, so workers would not wait out a long schedule for the initial boost.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay at or near the minimum wage — restaurants, retail stores, agriculture, and small businesses — would bear roughly 39% higher hourly labor costs at full phase-in. Garment and hospitality employers in the Northern Mariana Islands would face a wage floor rising from $3.55 toward the federal level. Some portion of the cost would reach consumers through prices, and some employers could respond by cutting hours or entry-level jobs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retailers, and CNMI garment makers

drawbacks.text: Raising the wage floor about 39% over roughly 18 months sharply increases labor costs for businesses that pay at or near the minimum, and opponents of such increases typically argue that faster, larger hikes reduce entry-level hiring and push some small employers toward automation or closure.

Even under the bill's own schedule, a full-time minimum-wage worker would have waited nearly a year and a half for the full $2.00 raise, and the gradual CNMI phase-in would leave island workers well below the federal floor for years.

Because the wage floor applies uniformly, it does nothing for workers in lower-cost regions whose employers already pay above $7.15, while imposing the same increase on businesses in cheaper labor markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is the classic one: a clear, sizable pay raise for the lowest-paid workers against higher labor costs for the businesses that employ them, spread partly into prices. The design is moderate — phased steps, a long transition for the Northern Mariana Islands — which softens the employer cost but delays the benefit. The larger problem is that it never happened at all: the $5.15 wage floor stayed in place throughout this Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to its Workforce Protections subcommittee, and the House never held a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sherwood Boehlert, a moderate Republican, introduced the bill on July 25, 2005, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
Fifteen additional House Republicans signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill 16 Republican backers in a House that chamber's own party controlled.
On October 12, 2005, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no further action of any kind.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 with the bill still in subcommittee, so the minimum wage increase never came to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers paying at or near the minimum wage and the Northern Mariana Islands' garment industry kept the status quo, while minimum-wage workers went without the raise and the wage floor stayed at $5.15.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Minimum-wage employers and CNMI garment makers

for.name: Rep. Sherwood Boehlert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the minimum wage to $7.15 and extend it to the Northern Mariana Islands.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Workforce Protections subcommittee and never held a hearing or markup on it.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party leadership of the 109th House
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so positions were never tested on the floor; all 16 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, but the Republican-controlled committee never moved the bill either.

industries.note: The bill would raise their hourly wage floor from $5.15 to $7.15 in three steps, increasing labor costs roughly 39% at full phase-in. Their interest in blocking the bill runs directly against the raise the lowest-paid workers would receive.

industries.industry: Northern Mariana Islands garment and hospitality employers
industries.note: The bill ends the islands' exemption from the federal minimum wage, phasing workers up from $3.55 an hour in $0.50 steps every six months. The CNMI wage exemption had long shielded the islands' labor-intensive garment industry from the federal floor.
